query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: Grain-boundary segregation and precipitation in high-entropy alloys lead to toughness degradation due to localized chemical fluctuations and resultant nanoscale precipitates.
generation.mechanism: Localized chemical fluctuations and resultant nanoscale precipitates
generation.predicted_outcome: Emergence of brittle behavior and toughness degradation
generation.baseline: Initial single-phase high-entropy alloy microstructure and mechanical properties
generation.boundary: Temperature and loading conditions beyond which brittle behavior emerges
generation.uncertainty: Insufficient evidence to determine the specific mechanisms governing toughness degradation in high-entropy alloys

falsification_experiment.design: Controlled comparison of thermally treated and mechanically loaded high-entropy alloy samples
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no correlation is found between grain-boundary segregation, nanoscale precipitation, and toughness degradation, the hypothesis is falsified
